title: Becoming Muslim
hook: a person becomes Muslim by sincerely saying the shahada, often before witnesses

segments.voice: Yesterday, risalah, the message and the one sent with it, and your line: he shows the way. Which sunnah did you try, and did it change the moment? Day one thousand sixty-seven.

The Friday prayer is over, and nobody is leaving yet. A woman stands near the front, a little pale, holding a folded card she doesn't end up needing. The imam says the words a phrase at a time, and she repeats them after him. Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah. Wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah. Then the room says Allahu akbar, and a line forms of people who have never met her, waiting to hug her or shake her hand. That's one way it happens. What actually made her Muslim, in that moment, was invisible.
screen: `THE WORDS, A PHRASE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: In Islam, a person becomes Muslim by saying the two sentences of the shahadah and meaning them. No course to pass first, no fee. Just the testimony, said sincerely. First, it has to be free. The Qur'an says plainly, in Pickthall's translation: "There is no compulsion in religion." A testimony forced out of someone is not a testimony at all. Second, the sincerity lives where no one can check it. Sahih Muslim records a hard story. In a battle, a companion named Usama overtook an enemy fighter, who said la ilaha illallah. Usama struck him anyway, thinking he only said it out of fear. When the Prophet heard, he asked him, and kept asking: did you split open his heart, to know whether it said it or not? People can hear the words. Only God sees the heart. So the community takes the words at face value, and leaves the rest to God. Third, the witnesses. The shahadah is often said in front of others, at a mosque, with friends, sometimes with a certificate afterward for practical needs. The witnesses can't see the heart either. What they can do is know, and welcome: show up, teach the prayer, invite someone to iftar in Ramadan. Fourth, a beginning, not a finish line. The person who says it on Friday will still need to learn how to pray on Saturday. Some teachers point here to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: actions are judged by intentions. The intention comes first, the learning follows, and nobody expects the new Muslim to know it all on day one.

The practice: welcome someone new. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time you were new somewhere: a school, a job, a family, a country. Remember who made it easier, and what exactly they did. Maybe a name remembered, a seat saved, a question answered without a sigh. Now bring to mind someone who is new right now, perhaps someone who has recently become Muslim, perhaps a newcomer of any kind. If you pray, you can ask good for them. Then decide one small welcome you could give this week. The bell holds the time.
Becoming Muslim. Two sentences, said freely and meant, with the heart left to God and the welcome left to the community. Today's word.
Your line: said sincerely. Today, give the welcome you chose, a message, a seat, a name remembered. Tomorrow, what the testimony asks of the one who says it. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

howItsDone: A person becomes Muslim by sincerely saying the shahadah, often at a mosque before witnesses, after which the community usually greets them and helps them learn the prayer and the basics of practice.

notes: Editor: hook opener changed so it doesn't echo day 1054's 'Friday, in a big-city mosque'; Usama story now follows the hadith's repeated question instead of the added 'deeply troubled'; word line no longer puts the narrator inside the community ('the rest of us').
Usama story (Sahih Muslim 96) paraphrased, including 'deeply troubled'; the hadith has the Prophet repeating the question. Confirm the number and that telling a battle story here is appropriate.

Hook scene (repeating after the imam, takbir, people lining up to welcome) is described as 'one way it happens', not as a rule. Scholars differ on whether witnesses are needed for the shahadah to count; the script says only that it is often said before others and that witnesses cannot see the heart. Keeper may add the legal views.
'Sometimes with a certificate afterward for practical needs' (e.g. for travel to Mecca); confirm wording.
